maya-1.heard: Funny thing is, my job's named after a real person, a man who started doing it back in the late 1920s. Before him, people did a version of it backstage in theatres.

maya-2.heard: I usually start in a really quiet room. I'll get everything set up, have a look at what we're working on, then spend the day making noise.

maya-3.heard: People always ask if it's all done on a computer now some of it is but honestly doing it by hand often sounds much more believable

maya-4.heard: I've got far too many pairs of shoes, not nice ones either. It's more about the soles, each pair sounds a bit different when you walk.

maya-5.heard: There's a screen in front of me and a microphone nearby. Then there's gravel, wood, sand, all sorts of things on the floor. It looks quite odd.

maya-6.heard: Getting the sound right is only half of it. The timing has to be right as well, even when I'm using something completely different to make the noise.

maya-7.heard: Yesterday I was snapping vegetables for a fight scene. Then I changed shoes and walked back and forth for about an hour. That's a fairly normal day.

maya-8.heard: So, the footsteps and little rustles you hear in a film. I perform those sounds while watching the scene and we record them to match the picture.

jonah-1.heard: What I do goes back about 500 years. The story usually starts with a locksmith in Nuremberg. Back then, only the very rich could afford what he made.

jonah-2.heard: First thing I do is clear the bench. I know that sounds a bit fussy, but when the parts are this small you really do need to.

jonah-3.heard: People think I spend all day making new things most days I'm just trying to work out why something old isn't doing what it should

jonah-4.heard: I've got a pair of very fine tweezers and a little magnifier I wear over one eye. You get used to working like that after a while.

jonah-5.heard: There's a pale mat on my bench, with little trays for all the parts. If I drop a screw, that's it, I'm on the floor looking for it.

jonah-6.heard: You can replace a broken bit and still have the same problem. Usually there's something else wearing out, so I have to keep looking.

jonah-7.heard: Someone brought in their father's old one last week. He'd worn it for forty years. Hearing it tick again after I'd serviced it was lovely, actually.

jonah-8.heard: I repair mechanical watches, I take the movement apart, clean it, oil it and replace anything worn, then I check how well it's keeping time.

inez-1.heard: The first person to do my job in America stood out in a field with a couple of flags and a wheelbarrow. That was 1929. We've got slightly better equipment now.

inez-2.heard: There's always a handover first. I need to know what's going on, what the weather's doing, and whether anything's likely to change while I'm working.

inez-3.heard: People sometimes hear my voice and think it must be pretty quiet. I'm just keeping it calm. There can be a lot going on at once

inez-4.heard: My headset's probably the most important thing I use. I keep what I say short and clear, then I listen carefully to what comes back.

inez-5.heard: I've got a display with moving symbols on it. Each one has information I'm following, but I can't let one thing take all my attention.

inez-6.heard: You're always thinking a few minutes ahead. Where's everyone going to be? What happens if the weather changes? You can't just deal with what's in front of you.

inez-7.heard: We had a storm moving through today, we coordinated some route changes, and I was talking to pilots as they worked their way around it.

inez-8.heard: I'm an air traffic controller. I talk to pilots and coordinate aircraft movements, helping keep the planes safely separated in the airspace I'm responsible for.

theo-1.heard: People were doing my job in Egypt about four and a half thousand years ago. They carved it into temple walls. Honestly, some of it hasn't changed that much.

theo-2.heard: I check the weather before I make any plans. If it's cold and wet, I might leave things alone. A warm, calm day is much easier.

theo-3.heard: Everyone asks about the sweet stuff. And yeah, that's part of it. But mostly, I'm trying to keep a whole little community healthy through the year.

theo-4.heard: I've usually got my veil, a flat metal tool, and a smoker with me. You learn quite quickly that moving slowly is better than rushing in.

theo-5.heard: It's all outdoors, beside these rows of wooden boxes. You can lift frames out of them and get a proper look at what's happening inside.

theo-6.heard: I'm checking they've got enough food, looking for disease, and making sure the Queen's laying. You can't really tell all that from standing outside the box.

theo-7.heard: I lifted a frame today and found healthy brood, which was good to see. When we harvest honey later on, we'll leave enough stores for the colony.

theo-8.heard: I'm a beekeeper. I look after honey bee colonies, check their hives, and help keep them healthy. And when there's enough, I harvest some of the honey.

nadia-1.heard: 400 years ago, Dutch painters would spend days arranging a table before they painted it. What I do is sort of a modern cousin of that. It only became a real job about 70 years ago.

nadia-2.heard: I'll go shopping and buy 20 of the same thing. It looks ridiculous, but I might only find one that's the right shape or the right color.

nadia-3.heard: People say, well, doesn't it just need to taste good? Sure, but the people seeing my work can't taste it. They've only got the picture.

nadia-4.heard: I keep tweezers next to my chopping board. Sometimes I'll spend ten minutes moving one little leaf around. It's a very particular kind of patience.

nadia-5.heard: There's usually a camera right beside me. The lights get warm too, so anything that melts is a bit of a race against the clock.

nadia-6.heard: You can make something look beautiful on a plate, then look through the lens and it just doesn't work. I'm always checking what the camera sees.

nadia-7.heard: We were shooting a burger today. We went through a few buns, moved all the layers around, even adjusted some sesame seeds before the photographer was happy.

nadia-8.heard: I'm a food stylist. I prepare and arrange food for the camera, for things like adverts and cookbooks. My job is to make the dish look its best.

kenji-1.heard: There's a book from 13th century China that people in my field still mention, the first proper lab for my kind of work opened in France about a century ago, in an attic of all places.

kenji-2.heard: Before I start, I check the labels, the seals, all the paperwork. I need to know where a sample's been and who's handled it before me.

kenji-3.heard: It's nothing like it looks on TV, honestly. There's a lot more checking and waiting, and sometimes the answer really is, we don't know yet.

kenji-4.heard: The microscope gets all the attention, but clean gloves and separate containers matter just as much. I can't risk one sample coming into contact with another.

kenji-5.heard: Most of my days in a lab, looking at things collected somewhere else. We keep the space controlled so we're not accidentally adding anything to the samples.

kenji-6.heard: Two things can look alike without coming from the same place. I have to be really clear about that, especially when someone wants a definite answer.

kenji-7.heard: Today, I was comparing tiny fibers from two samples. I recorded what I found and wrote it up. That report might end up being discussed in court.

kenji-8.heard: I'm a forensic scientist. I examine physical evidence for investigations, document what I find, and sometimes explain the results and their limits in court.
